messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological PTSD case vignettes.
Write in third person as a realistic personal narrative —
the kind a therapist might write after getting to know a patient over several sessions.
The vignette should describe a real person's lived experience,
not a clinical report or a list of symptoms.
Vignettes should be 500–700 words.

Important:
- Tell the story chronologically — from the traumatic event to the present
- Show symptoms through what the patient thinks, feels, and does
- Integrate the patient's occupation naturally into the story
- Do NOT end with a diagnosis or treatment recommendation

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.

Patient demographics:
- Age: 22
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Product Manager
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 36

Mateo presents as a meticulously put-together young man, his posture straight, his clothes neat. At 22, he carries the quiet confidence of someone who has achieved success early. He landed a coveted Product Manager role straight out of college and speaks about his work—organizing sprints, building roadmaps, interfacing with engineering teams—with a detached precision. It’s this same precision that seems to crumble when he speaks about anything that happened more than six months ago.

Six months ago, he was on a long-overdue trip to visit his grandmother in his family’s home country. He describes the first week as idyllic—the smell of his grandmother’s cooking, the warm nights spent on the veranda, the familiar cadence of his native language. He was mapping out a new feature release on his laptop one afternoon when the air began to hum with a low, unfamiliar rumble. It wasn't thunder. Within an hour, the hum had become the percussive, ground-shaking reality of artillery.

He and his grandmother spent the next four days in her small, musty basement. For Mateo, a man whose life revolved around Gantt charts and predictable outcomes, the experience was a complete system failure. There was no plan, no escape route, no one to escalate to. There was only the concrete floor, the smell of damp earth and fear, and the deafening, unpredictable rhythm of the shelling. He remembers one blast, terrifyingly close, that blew out the small basement window, showering the far wall with glass and dirt. In that moment, he was certain they were going to die, and his only thought was a loop of failure: he, the planner, had brought himself here and trapped his grandmother with him.

They were eventually evacuated by a humanitarian convoy. The journey back to the U.S. was a blur of checkpoints and crowded buses. When he finally walked into his own quiet, orderly apartment, the silence was as jarring as the explosions had been. He told himself he was fine, lucky even. He threw himself back into his work, determined to regain control.

But control remains elusive. His world, once a predictable series of inputs and outputs, is now a minefield of potential threats. The sudden roar of a garbage truck on his street sent him diving to the floor behind his sofa last week, his heart hammering against his ribs, the metallic taste of dust inexplicably filling his mouth. He stayed there for ten minutes, shaking, long after the truck had gone.

At work, his performance is suffering. He sits in meetings, trying to focus on user stories and KPIs, but a loud laugh from the sales department or the slam of a door down the hall can make him flinch violently. He finds himself unable to sit with his back to the door in the open-plan office, constantly scanning the room and tracking the movements of his colleagues. This hypervigilance is exhausting, leaving him irritable and drained. His manager noted his “lack of focus” in their last one-on-one. He feels a profound sense of shame, as if he’s failing at this, too.

He has started avoiding things. He no longer goes to bars with friends—the sudden noises and crowds are too much. He screens calls from his family because hearing his grandmother’s voice, while comforting, also brings him right back to the suffocating darkness of the basement. He spends most of his evenings alone in his apartment, the shades drawn, trying to work but mostly just staring at the screen. He speaks of his life before the trip as if it belonged to someone else entirely—a capable, ambitious young man whose roadmap has been completely erased. Now, he feels stuck, a ghost haunting the edges of a life he no longer knows how to manage.
